blocks.text: As the land of the Hebrews is most fertile in locusts, so is their language in names for locusts. For, to say nothing of the Talmudic ones, which occur in great number, in the writings of the Prophets alone the doctors count ten. They are: 1. ארבה arbe. 2. גוב gob, or גובי gobai. 3. גזם gazam. 4. חגב chagab. 5. חנמל chanamal. 6. חסיל chasil. 7. חרגל chargal. 8. ילק jelek. 9. סלעם solam. 10. צלצל [col. 442] tselatsal. Since the origins of these words are for the most part little known, we have thought it worthwhile to explain them here in passing: for the thing lies hidden in the words, and much that pertains to the nature of these animals is drawn out of their names.

I. The first, ארבה arbe, Aben Ezra on Leviticus rightly derives מלשון רבוי, from the meaning of multitude. For רבה raba means to be much or to be multiplied. Hence ארבה arbe, with Aleph prefixed, as often. Nor is it obscure why locusts took their name from abundance, since no animal is more prolific. Hence of the Midianites [col. 443] Iud. VI, 5: And they came like locusts, they and their camels without number. And Iudic. VII, 12: They were spread out in that valley like locusts in multitude. And Psal. CV, 34: And the locust came, and the bruchus, of which there was no number. And Ierem. XLVI, 23, of the trees of the forest: Because they are more than locusts, and there is no number of them. And LI, 14: Surely I will fill you with men, as with bruchi. And Ioel. I, 6, of the locusts that were to lay waste Judaea: A nation is come up against your land, strong and without number. And Nahum III, 15: Be as numerous as the bruchus, as numerous as the locust. And [III, 252] Iudith. II, 11: They gathered to them like locusts, and like the sand of the earth: for they were innumerable for multitude. And of the locusts of Egypt, Exod. X, 5: They shall cover the face of the earth, so that no one can see the earth. Hence Jerome on Joel: What is more innumerable than locusts? And the common proverb of the Arabs, مال كالدبا [māl ka-l-dabā] Wealth (or cattle) like locusts, that is, very abundant. But these things are known to everyone ^{(1)}.

II. But why the locust is called in Hebrew גוב gob, or גובי gobai, Amos VII, 1. and Nahum III, 17., and in Arabic جاب [jāb] gab, or جابي [jābī] gabi, I would still not know, had not the Arabs taught me, among whom the verb جبا [jabā] gaba means to emerge from the earth, which is characteristic of locusts. Aristotle, History book 5, chapter 28: Ὅταν τέκωσιν (αἱ ἀκρίδες) ἐνταῦθα γίνονται σκώληκες ὠοειδεῖς, οἳ περιλαμβάνονται [Hotan tekōsin (hai akrides) entautha ginontai skōlēkes ōoeideis, hoi perilambanontai] [III, 253] ὑπό τινος γῆς λεπτῆς, ὥσπερ ὑφ᾽ ὑμένος· ἐν ταύτῃ δὲ ἐκπέτονται [hypo tinos gēs leptēs, hōsper hyph᾽ hymenos; en tautē de ekpetontai]. When the locusts have laid, there arise there egg-shaped grubs, which are enclosed by a very thin earth, as by a little membrane, from which they fly out. Gaza: When this is split open, the locusts emerge and fly out. Pliny, book 11, ch. 29: These lay their eggs, packed close, in the ground in autumn, letting down the stalk of their spine. They last through the winter under the ground; and at the following end of spring they send forth small ones, etc. To the same I refer the fact that by the Ethiopians and Troglodytes locusts are called አንበጣ፡ anbat. For in Arabic نبط [nabaṭa] nabata is to gush forth, and to issue and emerge from the earth. This indeed is proper to springs, but it is also transferred to other things καταχρηστικῶς [katachrēstikōs] ^{(2)}.
